title: 22. Interview: Authorization
summary: Interview Q&A for Authorization — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Authorization interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the principle of least privilege, and why is deny-by-default the safer posture?
**Answer:** The principle of least privilege says that every identity — human, service, or machine — should hold only the permissions necessary to perform its job, and no more. Operationally this means starting from zero permissions (deny by default) and granting what is observed to be needed, rather than starting broad and tightening after a breach. Deny-by-default is safer because a missing permission surfaces immediately as a 403 that the team can triage and grant; an over-permissive posture silently enables the next breach. The 2019 Capital One incident — where a single compromised WAF role reached 700+ S3 buckets because of broad `s3:GetObject` grants — is the textbook example of what least-privilege violations look like in production. AWS IAM Access Analyzer, GCP IAM Recommender, and Kubernetes tools like rbac-lookup exist specifically to surface these violations continuously, because manual review cannot keep up with the rate of policy change in modern infrastructure.
**Visual:**
```
default-allow       |     default-deny
   |                |        |
   v                |        v
 breach happens     |    403 -> triage -> grant
 then tighten       |    (visible, fast, safe)
```

### Q2. What is the difference between RBAC and ABAC, and when would you choose one over the other?
**Answer:** RBAC (role-based access control) assigns permissions to roles, then assigns roles to users; a user's effective permissions are the union of permissions across all their roles. It scales well when the number of roles is small and stable (tens to low hundreds) even if the user count is large. AWS IAM managed policies like `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` and Kubernetes' `cluster-admin`/`admin`/`edit`/`view` are textbook RBAC. ABAC (attribute-based access control) evaluates policies over attributes of the principal, resource, action, and environment — "allow read on docs where `doc.dept == user.dept AND request.ip in corp_range AND time in business_hours`." ABAC scales better when you need fine-grained, multi-tenant, or hierarchical permissions, because the policy count stays small while the attribute space captures combinatorial detail. Choose RBAC when permissions cluster cleanly around job functions; choose ABAC (or RBAC+ABAC hybrid, the most common real-world shape) when the same role needs to behave differently per resource attribute or environment.
**Visual:**
```
RBAC:   user -> role -> perms on resource_pattern
ABAC:   user.attrs + resource.attrs + env -> policy -> allow/deny
Hybrid: RBAC grants the (role, action, resource) edge;
        ABAC rules refine it (deny outside business hours, etc.)
```

### Q3. Why are wildcards dangerous in authorization policies, and how do you mitigate the risk?
**Answer:** Wildcards (`*` in AWS IAM, `*` in Kubernetes RBAC verbs/resources, `.*` in regex) collapse the policy's specificity, often silently. A policy like `s3:*` on `*` grants every S3 action on every bucket in the account — useful for prototyping, catastrophic in production, because a compromise of any holder pivots to all data. The 2017 Equifax breach and the 2019 Capital One breach both featured wildcard-related escalation. Mitigations: ban wildcards in CI by linting policies (tools like `iamlint`, `checkov`, `tfsec`); scope resources as narrowly as possible (`arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/finance/*` rather than `*`); require explicit allow-listing for sensitive actions (`s3:DeleteBucket`, `iam:CreateUser`, `ec2:RunInstances`); require a second reviewer for any policy containing `*` in production; and use AWS IAM Access Analyzer continuously to flag any policy that grants access to external principals or to all resources. When wildcards are unavoidable, narrow the action list as much as possible.
**Visual:**
```
BAD:   s3:* on *
       -> 1 breach reaches ALL buckets
GOOD:  s3:GetObject on arn:...:finance-prod/*
       -> blast radius = 1 prefix
```

### Q4. What is the difference between ACLs and RBAC, and when are ACLs actually better?
**Answer:** ACLs (access control lists) attach a list of (principal, permission) pairs directly to each resource; the resource is the source of truth for who can access it. RBAC attaches permissions to roles and roles to users; the role is the indirection layer between principals and resources. ACLs scale poorly when the principal set is large or volatile — granting 10,000 engineers access to a new bucket via ACLs requires 10,000 writes, while RBAC requires one role assignment per user. However, ACLs are better when the per-resource principal set is genuinely small and per-resource overrides matter: POSIX file permissions on a single config file, S3 object-level ACLs for one-off shares, DynamoDB item-level access for collaboration features. The right answer is usually hybrid — RBAC for the 95% case, ACLs for per-resource exceptions layered on top — and many systems (AWS S3 with bucket policies + IAM roles, Google Drive with role-based sharing + per-file ACLs) are designed exactly this way.
**Visual:**
```
ACL:    resource -> [alice: read, bob: write]   (per-resource list)
RBAC:   resource <- role <- [alice, bob]         (role indirection)
hybrid: RBAC default + per-resource ACL overrides
```

### Q5. How does policy-as-code change the operational model for authorization?
**Answer:** Policy-as-code expresses authorization rules in a real language — Rego (OPA), Cedar (Amazon AVP, GitHub), Sentinel (HashiCorp), or XACML — stored in version control, peer-reviewed via pull requests, and unit-tested in CI. This replaces the older model where policies were configured in admin consoles, changed without review, and audited only after incidents. The shift has three operational consequences. First, every policy change becomes an auditable, reviewable artifact with a clear author and timestamp, satisfying SOC 2 and ISO 27001 access-control requirements. Second, CI can run linting (`iamlint`, `conftest`) and policy tests before merge, catching typos and over-permissive patterns before they ship. Third, the policy engine itself can be deployed as a sidecar or centralized service, giving every microservice a consistent enforcement point with decision logging. The cost is that Rego and Cedar are real languages with subtle semantics, and teams must invest in training — but the alternative (policies as untracked console configuration) is the source of countless production incidents.
**Visual:**
```
developer writes policy.rego
   |
   v
PR review + CI: conftest test + iamlint
   |
   v
merge -> OPA sidecar receives bundle
   |
   v
every API call: sidecar decides allow/deny + logs
```

### Q6. What is the relationship between authentication, authorization, and audit in a zero-trust architecture?
**Answer:** Zero trust replaces the older "trusted internal network" model with the assumption that no implicit trust is granted based on network location. Every request, regardless of source, must authenticate, must be authorized against the specific resource it targets, and must be logged for audit. The three pillars therefore become continuous rather than one-time: authentication is re-verified on every request (mTLS for service-to-service, short-lived tokens for users), authorization is evaluated per action against current attributes (not cached from yesterday's role assignment), and audit captures every decision for forensic review. Google's BeyondCorp, Zscaler ZTNA, and Cloudflare Access are commercial implementations. The benefit is that a compromised laptop inside the corporate VPN no longer reaches every internal service — it still has to authenticate and authorize per resource. The cost is engineering complexity: every service must enforce the three pillars, the policy engine becomes a critical path component, and the audit log volume grows by orders of magnitude.
**Visual:**
```
request -> AUTHN (mTLS/token)
       -> AUTHZ (per-action policy)
       -> AUDIT (log every decision)
       -> resource
       (every time, regardless of network)
```

### Q7. What is role explosion, and how do ABAC and grouping mitigate it?
**Answer:** Role explosion is the failure mode where an RBAC system grows to thousands of narrowly-differentiated roles because the role abstraction cannot express fine-grained variation. A bank that needs `Teller-East`, `Teller-West`, `Teller-Weekend`, `Teller-Supervisor-East`, and so on ends up with one role per (job × region × shift × seniority) cell, which is unmanageable to assign, audit, and review. ABAC mitigates this by moving the variation into attributes rather than roles: one `Teller` role plus attributes like `region=east`, `shift=weekend`, `supervisor=true` lets a single policy express the same matrix. Grouping strategies (AWS permission sets, Azure AD administrative units, Kubernetes namespaces) provide another mitigation by scoping role bindings to a subset of resources rather than the entire cluster. The most common real-world pattern is RBAC for the coarse job-function layer plus ABAC for the fine-grained context layer, which keeps the role count manageable while still expressing the necessary variation.
**Visual:**
```
RBAC only:    Teller-East, Teller-West, Teller-Weekend-East, ... (1000 roles)
RBAC + ABAC:  Teller role + attrs (region, shift, supervisor) -> 1 role
RBAC + ns:    Teller role scoped to namespace=east -> 1 role
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your team has accumulated 8,000 IAM roles across 30 AWS accounts. Auditors are unhappy. How do you rationalize?
**Answer:** Start by instrumenting actual usage: enable AWS IAM Access Analyzer and CloudTrail in every account, run for 30 days, and correlate every `AssumeRole` and API call back to the principal that made it. Roles that were never used in the window are candidates for removal; roles that were used only by one service are candidates for narrowing. Cluster the remaining roles by their effective permission sets — many "different" roles will turn out to grant the same permissions and can be consolidated into one managed role. Establish a tagging standard (owner, cost-center, sensitivity) and require it on every role; any untagged role after a deadline is auto-deleted. Long term, migrate from long-lived roles to short-lived STS sessions issued by an identity provider (Okta, Azure AD) so the role count stops growing with headcount. Finally, schedule quarterly access reviews where each role's owner must justify continued existence, and use IAM Access Analyzer's unused-access findings to drive the cleanup queue. The goal is to drive the role count down by an order of magnitude, not to perfection.
**Visual:**
```
8000 roles
   |
   v
Access Analyzer + CloudTrail (30d)
   |
unused? delete  |  used? narrow + cluster
   |            |
   v            v
tag standard    managed roles only
   |
quarterly review keeps count flat
```

### Q2. A developer accidentally pushed an IAM policy with `s3:*` on `*` to a production account via Terraform. It shipped. What is your response?
**Answer:** Immediately roll back the Terraform change by reverting the PR and applying, which removes the over-permissive policy. Then enable AWS IAM Access Analyzer to scan for any resource that may have been accessed using the policy during the window it was live, and pull CloudTrail logs for `AssumeRole` events on that role in the same window — if any unexpected principal assumed it, treat that as an active incident and invoke IR. Add a guardrail so this cannot recur: a CI check (using `checkov`, `tfsec`, or `iamlint`) that fails any Terraform plan containing `Action = "*"` or `Resource = "*"` unless explicitly allow-listed with a justification comment. Add an SCP (service control policy) at the organization level that denies `s3:*` on `*` for any role not on an explicit exception list, so even a malicious or careless change cannot ship. Finally, conduct a blameless post-mortem on why the PR was approved without catching the wildcard, and add the lint rule as a required status check on the Terraform repo.
**Visual:**
```
ship -> revert PR + terraform apply
   |
   v
Access Analyzer + CloudTrail scan for misuse
   |
   v
CI: checkov / iamlint blocks wildcards
SCP at org level denies s3:* on * (hard guardrail)
post-mortem: PR review process updated
```

### Q3. You are designing authorization for a multi-tenant SaaS where customers want fine-grained per-team permissions. RBAC or ABAC?
**Answer:** Multi-tenant SaaS with per-team permissions is the textbook case for a hybrid RBAC-plus-ABAC model, often backed by something like Google Zanzibar or Amazon Verified Permissions. Pure RBAC explodes: per customer × per team × per role you end up with millions of role bindings, and changing team structure requires rewriting all of them. Pure ABAC handles the variation elegantly — a policy "allow read on doc where `doc.tenant == user.tenant AND doc.team == user.team AND user.role in {editor, admin}`" — but authoring and debugging Rego or Cedar at scale requires investment. The hybrid pattern is: use RBAC for the coarse, well-understood job-function layer (viewer/editor/admin) so customers see familiar role pickers in the UI; layer ABAC on top for the tenant and team scoping, so the same `editor` role behaves correctly in each tenant without exploding the role count. Implement this behind a centralized policy service with decision logging, and cache decisions aggressively (Zanzibar's "leaped" caches) because the policy engine becomes a hot path.
**Visual:**
```
RBAC:  viewer / editor / admin (per customer)
ABAC:  doc.tenant == user.tenant
       doc.team  == user.team
hybrid = same roles, scoped by ABAC attrs
   |
policy service (Zanzibar / AVP) + cache
```

### Q4. Your Kubernetes cluster has 200 service accounts with cluster-admin because "it was easier." How do you fix this without breaking production?
**Answer:** Start by inventorying which service accounts actually use which APIs — patch each pod to log the authenticated identity, or use audit logging in the API server to correlate each request to the requesting service account. For each service account, identify the resources and verbs it actually accesses over a 30-day window, then craft a narrow Role or ClusterRole that grants only those (start strict — a 403 in staging is the discovery mechanism). Apply the new role in a non-production cluster first, watch for breakage, fix, then roll to production with the previous cluster-admin binding still in place as a fallback. Once the new role is verified for a week, remove the cluster-admin binding. Long term, enforce that no service account can hold cluster-admin via an OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno admission policy that rejects the binding at apply time. Also enable Kubernetes' short-lived service-account tokens (1.21+) so even a leaked token has a 90-minute expiry rather than a multi-year lifetime.
**Visual:**
```
audit log -> per-SA API usage
   |
craft narrow role (start strict)
   |
staging -> fix 403s -> prod (with fallback)
   |
remove cluster-admin binding
   |
Gatekeeper: deny cluster-admin at admission
```

### Q5. Your auditors want a list of every user who can access the production database. How do you produce it?
**Answer:** This question sounds simple but is hard because production database access is usually layered: human users federate through an IdP, assume an IAM role, then use that role to assume a database role via IAM database authentication or a secrets manager. Start by enumerating the database roles that have production access (usually one or two — `app_rw`, `dba`). Trace each database role back to the IAM role(s) that can assume it (via `rds-db:connect` permissions or secrets-manager read policies). Then trace each IAM role back to the IdP groups that can assume it (via `AssumeRole` trust policies). Finally, query the IdP for the current members of each group. The result is a four-level join — IdP user → IdP group → IAM role → DB role — and the auditors care about the leaf users. Implement this as a script that runs weekly and writes to a dashboard, because the answer changes whenever someone joins, leaves, or changes roles. Treat any access path that bypasses this chain (a hard-coded service account, a direct DB password in a config file) as a finding to remediate.
**Visual:**
```
DB role  <-  IAM role  <-  IdP group  <-  IdP user
  |              |             |             |
  v              v             v             v
rds-db:connect  AssumeRole    group members (the leaves)
   trust policy
```

### Q6. You are building a feature where users can share individual files with external users (like Google Drive). How do you model the authorization?
**Answer:** This is the Google Drive / Dropbox sharing model and is best implemented as an ACL-on-top-of-RBAC pattern, often backed by a relationships graph like Google Zanzibar or SpiceDB. The file's effective permissions are the union of: (1) inherited permissions from the parent folder's role bindings (so a folder shared with `team-eng@company.com` gives every team member access to every file inside), and (2) direct ACL entries on the file itself (`alice@example.com: editor`, `external-user@partner.com: viewer`). Store the relationships as tuples `(file, ancestor, folder)`, `(folder, viewer, group)`, `(group, member, user)` in a graph that the policy engine can traverse, so computing "who can read this file" is a graph expansion rather than a recursive SQL query. For external sharing specifically, capture the share's expiry, the sharer's identity (for audit), and whether the share requires the recipient to authenticate (rather than a public link). Add abuse protections: rate-limit share creation, flag anomalous bulk sharing, and notify the file owner when a share is created.
**Visual:**
```
folder: team-eng (viewer)
   |
   +-- file A  + direct ACL: external@partner.com (viewer)
   +-- file B
   +-- subfolder: team-finance (editor)
              |
              +-- file C

effective perms on A = inherited(team-eng:viewer)
                   + direct(external@partner.com:viewer)
```

### Q7. Your service makes 50 sub-requests per inbound API call. The policy engine adds 5 ms per check, killing latency. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** First, measure where the 5 ms goes — network round-trip to a centralized OPA, Rego evaluation time, or attribute lookup. Most of the cost is usually network, so co-locate the policy engine as a sidecar (OPA as a DaemonSet) and use a Unix socket or localhost HTTP, dropping round-trip to sub-millisecond. Second, cache decisions: the same (principal, action, resource) tuple within a short window (e.g., 30 seconds) should return the cached decision rather than re-evaluating, with cache invalidation when the underlying policy or role binding changes (Zanzibar's "zookie" / "leaped" cache pattern handles this). Third, push the principal's attributes into the JWT at issuance time so the policy engine does not have to do an attribute lookup per call. Fourth, batch: many policy engines (OPA's batch API, AVP's `IsAuthorizedWithToken`) accept multiple decisions in one call, collapsing 50 round-trips into one. Fifth, push enforcement closer to the data: row-level security in Postgres or column masking in BigQuery handles per-row authorization without an application-layer call at all. The target is single-digit milliseconds added per inbound request, even with 50 internal sub-requests.
**Visual:**
```
50 sub-requests x 5ms = 250ms (bad)
   |
sidecar (1ms) + cache (hit rate 90%) + batch (1 call)
   |
~5ms added per inbound request (good)
```
